newsitem.title: UK: U.S. Treasuries seen weathering U.S. payrolls data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries seen weathering U.S. payrolls data.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market is likely to weather Friday's U.S. payrolls data well and may even rally into the weekend, analysts said on Thursday.

And provided the financial markets' most watched figure does not provide too many surprises, prompting fears of central bank action to cool the economy down, the spread between 10-year Treasuries and German Bunds is seen sliding back below 100 basis points (one percentage point).

"Technically, the market is in better shape and if we get the fundamental data tomorrow, that will spark a reasonably sharp rally into the weekend," said Yamaichi international bond strategist Adam Chester.
Last week's barrage of hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan knocked the wind out of the market and left it better placed to cope with Friday's data.
"A lot of bad news is now priced into the market and it's trading towards the lows," said Chester.
The 10-year T-note future spiralled almost two points lower last Wednesday after Greenspan said the Fed might need to raise interest rates before inflation got worse.
Friday's labour market report is seen as the key to whether a rise will be sanctioned at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on March 25.
According to a Reuters survey, economists expect U.S. non-farm payrolls to rise by 230,000 in February, less than the 271,000 increase in January.
Average hourly earnings are seen rising 0.4 percent, up from January's 0.1 percent rise. The unemployment rate is expected to fall to 5.3 percent from 5.4 percent in January.
Analysts agreed the market would be spared a re-run of events last year when a rise of 705,000 in February non-farm payrolls -- later revised down to 624,000 -- hit Treasury bulls hard.
"There were exceptional circumstances last year but still, according to forecasts for tomorrow, all the risks are skewed to the upside," said Citibank bond strategist Michael Burke.

"We're not in the same situation," agreed Chester. "This January saw a 271,000 gain, which suggests the labour market is not suffering the same one-off distortion as last year." Payrolls fell by 66,000 in January 1996.
Nomura senior bond strategist Sonia Gibbs said the rise in payrolls would have to push 300,000 for the market to take exception.

"Unless we get payrolls way out of line, the market won't do too badly," she said. "The conciousness Greenspan is getting ready to raise rates is already priced in, so the number would have to be very bad to prompt selling."
She said the data might contribute to a little more spread narrowing and the 10-year T-note/Bund gap might dip to below 100 basis points from just over that level.
Both Gibbs and Chester suggested investors stick to the short end of the Treasury yield curve -- the relationship between yield and maturity -- depending on their risk-reward profile.
"On a relative value basis, the area which looks most oversold is the short end as the curve has flattened quite sharply since Greenspan's testimony last week," said Chester.
"The two- to 30-year spread has come in to around 70 basis points. Over the coming months I expect the curve to steepen back out to about 85 basis points as rate concerns subside."
Gibbs said dollar strength was likely to benefit the shorter end on balance and Japanese buying into the fiscal year-end might give it a boost.
Burke said he would choose holding cash or assets close to cash. "Given the flatness of the curve, the opportunity cost of holding cash is not so great," he added.
